title: Sausage and Mash with Caramelised Onions
subtitle: Pork sausages and buttery mash with slow-cooked onion gravy
excerpt: Sausage and mash with caramelised onions is a pub-menu standard that is equally good at home: browned sausages, creamy mashed potato, and a glossy onion gravy that takes about 30 minutes to develop its sweetness. The onion gravy is what lifts it from weeknight convenience to something you actually look forward to.
sourceNotes: Sausages with mashed potato is a British working-class staple that has appeared in pub menus since at least the early twentieth century. The caramelised-onion gravy is the British pub version of French sauce Lyonnaise; the combination of pork sausages with mash became embedded in British comfort food culture during the post-war period.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The onion gravy keeps in the fridge for 3 days and reheats well with a splash of stock to loosen it.

content.text: Sausage and mash with caramelised onions is a pub-dinner classic: good pork sausages browned in a pan, served on buttery mashed potato with a slow-cooked onion gravy. The gravy is the key element. It takes 25 to 30 minutes of patient, low cooking to take onions from raw to deeply sweet and golden; rushing that stage produces a thin, slightly bitter result rather than a proper, dark, glossy gravy.

items.prepNote: floury variety such as Maris Piper, peeled and quartered

content.text: Melt 30 g of the butter with {{olive-oil}} of oil in a wide frying pan over a medium-low heat. Add {{onion}} thinly sliced onions and the thyme sprigs if using. Stir to coat in the fat, then cook over a low heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the onions are deep golden brown and very soft. Do not rush this; low heat and patience are what produce the sweetness.
While the onions cook, place {{potato}} of potatoes in a large saucepan, cover with cold salted water, and bring to a boil. Cook for 18 to 20 minutes until tender when pierced with a knife.
In a separate pan over a medium heat with a little oil, cook {{sausages-pork}} sausages for 15 to 20 minutes, turning every few minutes, until browned all over and cooked through. Keep warm.
Finish the gravy and make the mash

When the onions are deep golden, remove the thyme sprigs and stir in {{plain-flour}} of plain flour. Cook for 1 minute, stirring, to cook out the flour taste. Pour in {{stock-beef}} of beef stock and add {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes until the gravy has thickened and become glossy. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Drain the potatoes and return to the hot pan over a low heat for 1 minute to drive off excess moisture. Mash thoroughly, then beat in {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and the warm milk until smooth and creamy. Season well with salt.
Spoon the mash onto warm plates, place 2 sausages on each, and pour the onion gravy over everything.

items.symptom: The onion gravy is thin and pale
items.cause: The onions were not cooked long enough at a low enough temperature.
items.fix: The onions need 25 to 30 minutes over a low heat. If they are colouring too quickly and catching on the bottom, reduce the heat further and add a splash of water.

items.cause: The potatoes were over-worked or a waxy variety was used.
items.fix: Use a floury potato such as Maris Piper or King Edward. Mash only until smooth; beating too long breaks the starch cells and produces a starchy, gluey texture.

items.cause: The heat was too high and the casings split before the interior cooked through.
items.fix: Cook sausages over a medium heat, not high. Turn them often and do not prick them; the skin contains the juices and helps the sausages stay plump.

items.cause: The onions caught on the bottom of the pan and scorched.
items.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water if the onions stick. Scraped brown bits add flavour; black bits add bitterness.

content.text: Sausage and mash is one of the foundational plates of British pub cooking. The caramelised onion version, sometimes called French onion gravy in pub menus, became the standard upgrade from plain meat gravy during the pub food revival of the 1990s and 2000s. Cumberland or Lincolnshire sausages both work well; the sweeter, herb-heavy Cumberland is the more common pub choice. The dish is good with peas or steamed greens on the side, or simply on its own.
